title: DID THE PATRIARCHS FOLLOW GOD’S IDEAL—OR THEIR CULTURE?
paragraphs: DID THE PATRIARCHS FOLLOW GOD’S IDEAL—OR THEIR CULTURE?

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob had Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So here is the uncomfortable question many Christians quietly wonder but rarely dare to ask: If these were men of God, why did their homes sometimes look more like the surrounding culture than the garden God designed?
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible.
We can read everything a biblical hero did and assume that because Scripture records it, God approved it.
Abraham did it.
Jacob did it.
David did it.
Solomon did it.
So surely it could not have been that wrong.
Right?
But then Jesus says something that changes the entire conversation.
He does not point us back to Abraham.
He does not point us back to Jacob.
He does not point us back to David.
He goes farther back.
Back before kings.
Before patriarchs.
Before Israel.
Before human traditions had centuries to accumulate.
Jesus takes us all the way back to creation.
And suddenly the question is no longer, “What did the patriarchs practice?”
The question becomes...
“What did God intend from the beginning?”
That distinction changes everything.
Because the Bible is brutally honest about its heroes.
It does not airbrush them.
It does not hide their family disasters to protect their reputations.
It lets Abraham become afraid.
It lets Jacob deceive.
It lets Moses lose his temper.
It lets David commit terrible sin.
It lets Peter deny Jesus.
And that honesty is one of the reasons Scripture is so powerful.
The Bible is not primarily the story of extraordinary people who were good enough for God.
It is the story of a holy God who remains faithful while working through deeply flawed human beings.
That means something uncomfortable but liberating:
Being used by God does not mean everything a person does represents the will of God.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that sentence for reasons having nothing to do with ancient marriage.
Maybe you love Jesus, yet there are pieces of your life that still resemble the culture around you more than Christ.
Maybe you inherited patterns you never questioned.
Maybe everyone in your family did it.
Maybe everyone in your church circle accepts it.
Maybe everybody around you calls it normal.
But “normal” and “biblical” have never been synonyms.

The patriarchs lived inside real ancient cultures, with customs concerning marriage, inheritance, fertility, household survival, servants, concubines, tribal alliances, and descendants. Scripture describes those realities with remarkable honesty.
But description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible can tell us what happened without telling us to imitate everything that happened.
And nowhere is that clearer than in the tangled households of Genesis.
Before Abraham ever took Hagar...
before Jacob ever woke beside Leah...
before Rachel gave Bilhah to her husband...
before kings accumulated wives...
there was Eden.
And Eden gives us the starting point.
Genesis 2:24 says:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’îš ’et-’āvîw wə’et-’immō, wədāvaq bə’ištō, wəhāyû ləvāsār ’eḥād.
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Look closely at the final Hebrew words:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
And the verb דָּבַק — davaq carries the idea of clinging, holding fast, adhering closely.
This is covenant language expressed through intimacy, loyalty, and union.
One man.
His wife.
Holding fast.
One flesh.
This is the picture before sin begins distorting everything.
Then something changes.
By Genesis 4, humanity is already east of Eden.
Violence is growing.
Pride is growing.
Sin is multiplying.
And then we meet Lamech.
Scripture says:
וַיִּֽקַּֽח־ל֥וֹ לֶ֖מֶךְ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֑ים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lō Lemeḵ shətê nāšîm.
“Lamech took two wives.”

That is the Bible's first explicit description of a man taking two wives, and its literary setting matters: Genesis 4 is tracing humanity's movement into violence and disorder after the fall. The text reports Lamech's two wives; it does not present a command from God establishing polygamy as the creation ideal.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because years later, Abraham enters the story.
God promises him descendants.
But the promise seems impossible.
Sarah cannot conceive.
Years pass.
Hope becomes painful.
And eventually Sarah proposes a solution.
Hagar.
Genesis 16 records Sarah telling Abraham to go to her Egyptian servant so that perhaps she could build a family through her.
Then comes one of those painfully simple biblical sentences:
Abram listened.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham as a wife.
Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately...
the household began bleeding.
Contempt entered the relationship.
Sarah blamed Abraham.
Hagar was mistreated.
Hagar fled.

The arrangement produced a child whom God saw, heard, cared for, and blessed with promises concerning his descendants—but the narrative never requires us to pretend the human choices surrounding his conception were God's original marital design. God even meets Hagar in her affliction, and Ishmael's name itself is connected with the truth that the LORD heard her suffering.
That is breathtaking.
God's compassion toward people caught in the consequences of human decisions does not mean God endorses every decision that put them there.
And that is where some of us misunderstand grace.
We think:
“God blessed me afterward, therefore what I did must have been right.”
Not necessarily.
Sometimes God's blessing is not His endorsement of your mistake.
Sometimes it is evidence of His mercy despite it.
Read that again.
God can redeem what He never commanded.
That truth runs through Scripture.
And maybe it runs through your story too.
Maybe you made decisions God never told you to make.
Maybe impatience spoke louder than faith.
Maybe loneliness chose for you.
Maybe fear chose for you.
Maybe lust chose for you.
Maybe ambition chose for you.
Maybe family expectations chose for you.
Maybe culture chose for you.
And somehow God still met you afterward.
Do not mistake His mercy for approval of everything behind you.
But do not mistake your failure for the end of your story either.
Because grace knows how to enter places human beings have complicated.
Jacob's household makes that painfully clear.
Jacob loves Rachel.
But through Laban's deception he receives Leah.
Then Rachel.
Then Bilhah.
Then Zilpah.
Children are born inside an atmosphere repeatedly marked by rivalry, jealousy, longing, competition, and pain.
One woman aches because she is unloved.
Another aches because she is barren.
Servants become part of a struggle over children.
Sisters compete.
Eventually the children themselves become caught inside family favoritism, culminating in Joseph's brothers selling him into slavery.
Yet somehow...
through this fractured household...
God forms the twelve tribes of Israel.
Does that mean the dysfunction was God's ideal?
No.
It means God's sovereignty is greater than human dysfunction.
There is a difference.
And if you miss that difference, you may read the Bible backward.
You may begin using God's ability to redeem broken situations as permission to create them.
Grace does not make sin wise.
Grace means sin does not get the final word.
Even Israel's kings were warned.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says concerning the king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
The warning is explicit: multiplying wives could turn the king's heart away.
Then Solomon arrives.
The man famous for wisdom eventually demonstrates the very danger the law warned about.
The tragedy is almost unbearable.
A man can possess extraordinary wisdom and still disobey what he knows.
And suddenly this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because knowing Scripture is not the same thing as surrendering to Scripture.
You can quote verses and still protect an idol.
You can understand theology and still rationalize compromise.
You can preach truth publicly while privately negotiating with something God has told you to surrender.
The patriarchs are not displayed before us because every decision they made deserves imitation.
Their stories repeatedly reveal something far more hopeful:
God's covenant faithfulness survives human weakness.
Then Jesus enters the conversation.
Religious leaders question Him about marriage and divorce.
Jesus could have begun with Abraham.
He could have cited Jacob.
He could have appealed to Israel's kings.
Instead He reaches behind centuries of cultural practice and says, in Greek:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς
ap’ archēs.
“From the beginning.”
Then He recalls creation: male and female, a man joined to his wife, the two becoming one flesh.
And when explaining Moses' concession concerning divorce, Jesus says:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs.
“But from the beginning it has not been this way.”
Jesus makes a distinction between accommodations made in a fallen world and the pattern embedded in creation.
Do you see it?
Jesus does not allow broken human history to redefine divine intention.
He goes back to the beginning.
That principle reaches far beyond marriage.
Culture asks:
“What is everyone doing?”
Jesus asks:
“What did God say?”
Culture asks:
“What can I justify?”
Jesus asks:
“What was God's heart?”
Culture asks:
“How close can I live to the line?”
Jesus calls us:
“Follow Me.”
And perhaps that is the real question hiding underneath this entire article.
Not merely...
Did the patriarchs follow God's ideal or their culture?
But...
Am I following God's ideal—or mine?
Because it is easy to analyze Abraham from thousands of years away.
Harder to examine ourselves.
We notice Hagar but ignore our own shortcuts.
We notice Jacob's household but excuse our own favoritism.
We notice David's appetites but rename ours “weakness.”
We notice Solomon's compromises while protecting the things slowly stealing our own hearts.
We say, “But everyone does it.”
So did ancient cultures.
We say, “But God understands.”
He does.
Better than you know.
And because He understands, He loves you too much to pretend bondage is freedom.
The Gospel does not call you to hide behind the failures of biblical heroes.
The Gospel calls you to Christ.
That is where this story becomes something far greater than a debate about patriarchal marriage practices.
Because every broken biblical household points toward humanity's deeper problem.
Sin.
Not merely “their” sin.
Ours.
The instinct to rewrite God's boundaries.
The desire to seize what we do not trust Him to provide.
The habit of choosing cultural approval over divine obedience.
The temptation to call something good simply because God has been merciful afterward.
And if Scripture ended there, we would all be exposed with nowhere to go.
But Scripture does not end with Abraham.
It does not end with Jacob.
It does not end with David.
It does not end with Solomon.
It leads to Jesus Christ.
The faithful One.
The obedient Son.
The One who does not merely tell sinners to clean themselves up.
He comes for them.
He bears sin.
He calls people to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He restores.
He transforms.
And at the cross, something astonishing happens:
our scandal meets His grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that says sin never mattered.
Grace purchased at terrible cost.
Grace with nail scars.
Grace that can look directly at what you did without pretending it was righteous...
and still say that everyone who comes to Christ in repentant faith can be forgiven.
This is why Christianity does not require us to sanitize its heroes.
Abraham does not have to be perfect.
Jacob does not have to be perfect.
David does not have to be perfect.
Peter does not have to be perfect.
Because Jesus is.
That is the center.
The Bible's credibility does not depend upon pretending its human characters never failed.
Its hope depends upon the faithfulness of God.
Maybe that is why this subject feels more personal than expected.
Because somewhere inside all of us is a place where culture has discipled us more deeply than we want to admit.
A relationship.
A secret habit.
Money.
Sex.
Status.
Pride.
Bitterness.
The approval of other people.
Something we learned to call normal because everyone around us stopped calling it dangerous.
And Jesus is still whispering across the centuries:
“From the beginning...”
Come back.
Not merely back to rules.
Back to God.
Back to truth.
Back to repentance.
Back to the One who made you.
Maybe you have made an Abraham decision—trying to manufacture what you should have trusted God with.
Maybe you have lived inside a Jacob household—carrying wounds created by favoritism, betrayal, rejection, or family chaos.
Maybe you have had a David moment—knowing better and choosing desire anyway.
Maybe you have lived like Solomon—slowly allowing things into your heart that eventually competed with God.
Then hear this carefully:
Their failures are not permission for yours.
But neither are your failures proof that redemption is impossible.
Jesus still rewrites stories.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
Grace is not Jesus pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is Jesus refusing to let the scandal have the final sentence.
That is the Gospel.
So be honest.
Has something in this exposed an area where you have been following culture while telling yourself you were following God?
Tell the truth.
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggle. But sometimes one honest sentence is the moment somebody stops pretending.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
The Bible faithfully records human brokenness without requiring us to call brokenness God's design.
Biblical giving is to be willing rather than coerced. But voluntary financial support of Gospel work is a meaningful way believers can help make ministry possible.
Talk about it.
Open your Bible.
Examine your life.
And above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because one day nobody will stand before Christ and successfully say,
“But Abraham did it.”
“But David did it.”
“But everybody around me did it.”
The question will never finally be whether our culture normalized something.
The question is whether we trusted the One who called us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The patriarchs had scars.
Their families had scandals.
Their decisions sometimes produced consequences lasting generations.
Yet God kept moving His promise forward until, through that astonishingly imperfect human family line, the Messiah came.
Jesus.
And that may be the most beautiful answer of all.
God did not wait for a flawless family tree before sending a Savior.
He sent the Savior because humanity desperately needed one.
So when you see scandal in Scripture, do not look away.
Look closer.
You may discover grace moving through the wreckage.
And when you see scandal in your own story, do not call evil good—but do not run from Christ either.
Repent.
Come home.
Let Him have what culture taught you to protect.
Let Him confront what you learned to excuse.
Let Him heal what other people's sins broke inside you.
Let Him forgive what you broke yourself.
Because the deepest lesson of the patriarchs is not that flawed people somehow earned God's approval.
It is that the faithfulness of God is greater than the failures of people.
And the same Christ who exposes what was never God's design is the Christ who stretches wounded hands toward sinners and says:
Come.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
